Pythagoras. Around five hundred and seventy to four hundred and ninety-five BCE. He was an Ionian Greek philosopher and mathematician who founded a mystical and scientific community in southern Italy. He taught that numbers are the fundamental principle of reality and that the cosmos is governed by mathematical harmony. His ideas on transmigration of souls, dietary restrictions, and the music of the spheres merged mathematics with religion in a unique vision.

Pythagoras was born on Samos, an Ionian island. Little of his life is certain—later accounts are heavily mythologized. He migrated to Croton in southern Italy and founded a quasi-religious community called the Pythagorean society, around five hundred and thirty-two BCE. The society was secretive, communal, and ascetic. Membership required initiation and vows of secrecy. It was persecuted, and Pythagoras was apparently killed by Croton citizens. The community scattered, but the philosophical tradition survived.

His core insight was mathematical. Numbers and their ratios are the ultimate stuff of reality. "All things are numbers," he taught. He discovered that musical intervals correspond to simple numerical ratios—an octave is two to one, a fifth is three to two. This connection between music and mathematics shaped Western thought profoundly. The theorem bearing his name—that in a right triangle, a squared plus b squared equals c squared—is foundational to geometry, though it was likely known earlier. He posited ten pairs of opposite principles organizing reality: odd and even, limited and unlimited, one and many. He conceived of the cosmos as spheres in mathematical harmony—the music of the spheres.

Pythagoras taught metempsychosis, the transmigration of souls. The soul is immortal and reincarnates through different bodies. He imposed dietary taboos, especially a ban on beans, and demanded ritual purification as spiritual disciplines. He viewed philosophy as purification of the soul, liberation from the cycle of rebirths. He combined mathematics—what we would call science—with mysticism and religion in a unified worldview.

He profoundly influenced Plato, especially Plato's theory of forms and his idea of a transcendent realm of numbers. The Pythagorean theorem is the foundation of Euclidean geometry. Pythagoreanism inspired mystical number symbolism and sacred geometry throughout Western esotericism. The Pythagorean society was the first philosophical community organized as a way of life, not merely an intellectual school. Plato's Academy imitated this model.
